title: Working with AI agents: Fix the framework, not the symptom
summary: First-principles and systems thinking are becoming the most valuable muscles to exercise when working with AI agents.

body.markdown: Imagine you're reviewing an interface built by an AI agent. You notice that a button is slightly taller than the input field next to it.
You could simply tell the agent to fix the height. It makes the adjustment, and the problem is gone.
But what if you approached it differently?

Instead of pointing out the height mismatch, you ask the agent to investigate the design system. You want to understand whether the components are following the same sizing conventions, whether they're referencing the right design tokens, and whether the implementation is adhering to the component library.
The agent discovers that the button and input field are referencing different height tokens. It fixes the underlying inconsistency, and the original mismatch disappears.
But there's a bigger benefit. Other components that you hadn't even noticed might have the same problem. They get fixed too.
You didn't ask the agent to fix the problem you saw. You asked it to fix the framework that produced the problem.

body.text: The symptom is not the problem.
Fixing the symptom vs fixing the framework

body.markdown: This distinction is not new. Good engineers, designers and problem solvers have always understood the importance of addressing root causes rather than symptoms.
But working with AI agents makes this distinction particularly valuable.
An agent can fix the height of a button. It can also investigate the design system, trace dependencies, identify inconsistencies, and make systemic improvements.
Both approaches are possible. The difference lies in how we frame the problem and what we understand about the framework we're working within.
The first approach produces a local fix. The second improves the conditions under which the product gets built.
Consider another example.

You notice that a particular screen takes five seconds to load. You could ask the agent to optimize that screen. But perhaps the problem is caused by how the application handles data fetching, state management, or rendering.
Fixing the screen might improve one experience. Fixing the underlying architecture could improve the performance of the entire application.

Or consider accessibility. You could ask an agent to fix accessibility issues in individual components as you encounter them. Alternatively, you could establish accessibility standards, incorporate them into component development, and build automated checks into the validation process.
The latter doesn't just help you fix accessibility issues. It helps prevent them from being introduced in the first place.
In each case, the difference isn't how well you instruct the agent. It's how deeply you understand the problem and the framework producing it.

body.text: But isn't this how we've always been supposed to work?

body.markdown: You might argue that none of this is new. We've always known that we should address root causes, build sound architectures, maintain design systems, and invest in quality. First-principles thinking and systems thinking aren't discoveries brought about by AI.
And you'd be right.
But there's a rather important distinction between knowing the right way to do something and being able to afford doing it.
In practice, working this way has often been prohibitively expensive.

Investigating the underlying cause of an inconsistency takes time. Refactoring an architecture to address a systemic problem takes considerably more effort than patching a bug. Maintaining design systems, documenting conventions, building validation mechanisms, and keeping everything aligned across a growing product all require sustained investment.
When faced with deadlines, competing priorities, and limited resources, we make compromises.

We fix the immediate problem instead of addressing the underlying cause. We introduce exceptions instead of improving the framework. We postpone refactoring. We skip documentation. We accept inconsistencies because fixing them everywhere is too expensive.
This is how technical debt, design debt, and all sorts of accumulated compromises come into existence.
It's not necessarily because we don't know better. Often, it's because the cost of doing better is too high at that moment.

body.text: We've always known what good product development looks like. We've just rarely been able to afford doing it consistently.

body.markdown: This is where AI fundamentally changes the equation.

Investigating an architecture, tracing dependencies, identifying inconsistencies, refactoring components, writing tests, documenting decisions, and validating implementations are all activities that agents can now help us accomplish at a fraction of the previous effort.
This doesn't make the work free, nor does it eliminate the need for expertise and judgment. But it changes the economics of doing it properly.
We can now afford to investigate problems more deeply, address them at their source, and improve the frameworks around them rather than repeatedly settling for local fixes.

body.text: AI is making it economically practical to be fundamentally better at how we work.
The muscle we need to exercise is changing

body.markdown: For a long time, professional expertise was closely associated with our ability to execute.

We developed proficiency in tools, techniques, processes and the craft of producing things. Knowing how to do something, understanding the steps involved, and being able to execute them efficiently were significant sources of professional value.
These skills remain valuable. But AI agents are changing how much of the execution we need to do ourselves.
The opportunity is to redirect that effort.

Instead of spending most of our energy figuring out how to execute a task, we can spend more time understanding why we're doing it, questioning the assumptions behind it, examining the framework it belongs to, and figuring out what would produce a fundamentally better outcome.
This requires a different kind of muscle.

**First-principles thinking** helps us reason about problems without being constrained by existing assumptions, conventions or the immediate symptoms we observe. It helps us understand the underlying problem and establish what we're actually trying to achieve.

**Systems thinking** helps us understand how different parts interact, how decisions affect one another, and where an intervention can create the greatest impact. It moves us beyond isolated tasks and toward improving the frameworks that produce the outcomes.
These two complement each other.
First principles help us understand what needs to change. Systems thinking helps us understand where and how to make that change.

And this is particularly important when working with agents. They can execute instructions, explore solutions, investigate dependencies and make changes across an entire codebase. But the quality of those interventions depends heavily on how well we understand the problem and the framework within which we're asking them to operate.
You can give an agent a very specific instruction and get exactly what you asked for. But that doesn't necessarily mean you've solved the right problem.
Sometimes the best instruction is not to fix the problem you've observed, but to investigate and improve the framework that allowed it to happen.

body.text: The bottleneck is shifting from our ability to execute to our ability to think about what should be executed.
The more complex the problem, the more this matters

body.markdown: A simple task can often be handled in isolation. A complex product cannot.
As a product grows, its components, architecture, interactions, requirements and dependencies become increasingly interconnected. Decisions made in one area can have consequences elsewhere.
This is where simply delegating more tasks to agents starts to break down.

You might have multiple agents working in parallel, producing code, creating components, implementing features and fixing bugs. But without a coherent understanding of the product and the frameworks governing its development, you can end up with inconsistencies, conflicting decisions and increasing amounts of rework.
More execution capacity doesn't necessarily translate into more progress.
What you need is a way to make all that execution work toward a coherent outcome.

This means establishing the foundations before and during execution: a clear understanding of the problem, sound product decisions, design and engineering conventions, well-defined constraints, and mechanisms to validate the work.
You need to think about how the pieces fit together, not just whether each individual piece works.
The interesting thing about working this way is that you can take on problems that would otherwise have been prohibitively complex, slow or expensive to solve.
You're not merely using agents to do more work. You're using them to make more ambitious work practical.
There's another aspect of this that I think is easy to overlook.
When you invest time understanding a problem and figuring out a better way to solve it, don't let that learning remain confined to the project or conversation where it happened.
Articulate it. Refine it. Turn it into something reusable.

For example, if you've figured out a better way to establish product requirements, capture the methodology. If you've developed a reliable approach to auditing design systems, codify it. If you've established conventions for how agents should plan and execute work, make those conventions reusable.

These don't have to be elaborate frameworks. Sometimes a concise instruction is enough. Sometimes it needs to become a skill, a workflow, an agent, a validation tool, or an entire interconnected system.
The important thing is that the articulation is rooted in the underlying problem rather than the specifics of an individual project.
That makes it reusable and largely project-agnostic.
Over time, you accumulate a collection of principles, skills, workflows, tools and conventions that reflect your understanding of how to work effectively with AI agents.

This is something I've been deliberately building through my own work. My collection of kits, skills, tools and workflows is an evolving representation of how I approach product development with AI agents.
It spans everything from product discovery and specification to agent orchestration, design-system discipline, implementation, validation and documentation.
It's not a collection of prompts to copy and paste. It's an accumulated methodology for getting work done well.
And the value compounds.
Every new project starts with a better foundation. Every new problem is an opportunity to refine that foundation. Every successful experiment can become part of how you approach future work.

body.text: Don't just accumulate prompts. Accumulate understanding.
Keep evolving your way of working

body.markdown: Of course, none of this is static.
AI models are improving. Agent harnesses are evolving. New capabilities are emerging. Things that required elaborate workflows yesterday might become native capabilities tomorrow.
Some of the conventions we've established will become unnecessary. Others will need to be rethought. New possibilities will emerge that change how we approach problems altogether.
So the goal isn't to create a definitive playbook and stick to it.
It's to continuously evolve your methodology.
Learn from your own experiences. Curate what others have discovered. Experiment with new capabilities. Challenge existing assumptions. Refine what works and discard what no longer does.
The collection should evolve alongside the technology.

And this is another reason why investing in understanding and articulating your approach is worthwhile. You're not just optimizing how you work with today's models. You're building a foundation that can adapt as the capabilities change.

It's easy to get caught up in the mechanics of working with AI agents. Which model to use, which harness is better, how to write instructions, how many agents to orchestrate, and how to automate more of the process.
These things matter, but they aren't the differentiator I'm talking about.
The real differentiator is how you think.

Can you look beyond the immediate problem and understand what's producing it? Can you question the assumptions behind an established approach? Can you understand the larger system, identify the right intervention, and direct agents toward a solution that improves more than just the instance in front of you?
And can you turn those learnings into reusable knowledge that makes your next attempt even better?
These are the muscles worth exercising.
AI agents give us unprecedented execution leverage. But the ability to reason from first principles and think in systems determines how effectively we use that leverage.
The result isn't simply getting more work done. It's being able to produce better outcomes, more consistently, and tackle levels of complexity that would previously have been impractical.

body.text: Working with AI agents, fix the framework, not the symptom.
